Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)

- Working diagnosis: Acute gastroenteritis with dehydration risk.
  - Supporting findings from transcript: Onset ~3 days ago with profuse watery diarrhea; crampy mid/low abdominal pain; nausea/vomiting (milk-triggered); feverish sensation; poor intake with fluids rapidly losing; no blood in stool; household contact with similar illness; patient currently not on regular medications.
  - DDx integration: DDx supports acute gastroenteritis as the leading diagnosis (viral > bacterial possible), with lactose intolerance/malabsorption and less likely IBD or colorectal cancer as considerations.
- Key differentials (consistent with transcript/DDx)
  - Acute viral gastroenteritis (high likelihood): Sudden-onset large-volume watery diarrhea, crampy pain, nausea/vomiting, feverish feeling; household transmission supports contagion.
  - Acute bacterial gastroenteritis / foodborne infection (medium likelihood): Similar illness pattern in household; fever and cramps present; no blood in stool.
  - Lactose intolerance or post-infectious lactase deficiency (medium likelihood): Milk-triggered vomiting and crampy diarrhea; could contribute to symptoms but not explanatory of fever/dehydration.
  - Inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn’s/Ulcerative Colitis) (low to medium likelihood): Diarrhea with cramps in young adult; less likely given acute 3-day course and lack of chronicity features.
  - Colorectal cancer (low likelihood given age 27; family history noted): Family history of colon cancer; age and acute presentation make primary cancer unlikely, but consider if symptoms persist or worsen.
- Summary working impression: Acute gastroenteritis with dehydration risk; most consistent with viral gastroenteritis; bacterial etiologies and lactose intolerance are plausible alternatives; cancer and IBD considered but less likely given the current acute pattern.
- Plan
  - Hydration: Emphasize clear fluids; consider oral rehydration with Diarolyte (OTC) to replace fluids and minerals; no prescription required for Diarolyte.
  - Diet: Start with clear fluids; progress to soft diet (soup, mashed foods) as tolerated; avoid heavy or dairy if vomiting persists.
  - Medications: Acetaminophen (paracetamol) for fever/pain as needed; dose/route/frequency not documented. Advise to avoid alcohol while ill.
  - Red flags and follow-up: If symptoms persist or worsen or dehydration develops, contact back within 48 hours; if dehydration signs emerge (dry mucous membranes, reduced urine output, dizziness), seek urgent assessment.
  - Investigations: Not currently indicated; stool testing not initiated at this time unless symptoms persist/worsen or red flags appear.
  - Education: Reassurance about likely self-limiting illness; importance of hydration and gradual reintroduction of foods; avoidance of alcohol; monitor for fever, persistent vomiting, inability to keep fluids down, or blood in stool (seek care promptly).
- Follow-up and recall: Return call/clinic follow-up if not improving within 48 hours; plan to reassess in 1–2 days.

- Education on chronic disease prevention and lifestyle modification: Hydration strategies; use of oral rehydration solution; proper nutrition during gastroenteritis; limit alcohol during illness.
- Patient health goals and priorities: Return to baseline function and ability to work if possible; maintain hydration; monitor symptoms.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx)

- Acute viral gastroenteritis
  - Likelihood: High
  - Justification: Sudden, profuse watery diarrhea with crampy abdominal pain, nausea/vomiting, feverish sensations; household contact with similar illness; young adult with otherwise healthy status.

- Acute bacterial gastroenteritis / foodborne infection
  - Likelihood: Medium
  - Justification: Similar illness in household for multiple days; fever and cramps; non-bloody diarrhea; duration aligns with possible bacterial etiology.

- Lactose intolerance / malabsorption
  - Likelihood: Medium
  - Justification: Vomiting triggered by milk; diarrhea with crampy pain; could contribute to symptoms, though systemic features more suggestive of infection.
